citations.quote: The University of Wurzburg Experimental Satellite 5 (UWE-5) mission is advancing model-based systems engineering methodologies through the development of a modular, real-time capable on-board software framework.

Designed for operation within a lightweight 128KB memory footprint, this framework integrates formalized system modelling, fault-tolerant architectures, and dynamic resource management, enabling CubeSat missions to autonomously maintain critical functions under strict power and computational constraints.

The framework undergoes rigorous validation and verification using a combination of hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) and software-in-the-loop (SIL) simulations, digital twin analysis, and subsystem-level testing. Initial tests confirm that hardware load limitations effectively prevent instability, while upcoming power consumption evaluations will assess the system's ability to dynamically adapt energy usage.

The UWE-5 is a CubeSat project whose objective is the demonstration of a K-/KA-band communications payload. The development teams are comprised of three different working groups at different universities, namely the Embedded Systems and Sensors for Earth Observation (ESSEO) group at the Julius-Maximilians- Universität Würzburg, the Satellite Communications and Radar Systems chair at the Julius-Maximilians- Universität Würzburg, and the Electronic Systems and Sensors chair at Brandenburgische Technische Universität Cottbus. The mission consists of two 3U CubeSats operating in Low Earth Orbit. The project is supported by the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and estimated to launch in 2027.

In the context of the CubeSat project, the stakeholders are the various developer groups responsible for developing the different subsystems, writing the application code and designing the hardware. Particular attention is paid to the interfaces between the hardware and software, and to communication between the subsystems.
The system model of the UWE-5 project represents a complex interaction between two satellites, external applications, and internal subsystems (see Fig. 1).

The software architecture of each subsystem is uniform and independent of the underlying hardware. Fig. 2 illustrates the system model of the onboard computer as an example. A shared library, KronOS, serves as middleware between the RTOS and the process logic. The interfaces between software layers are defined through well-specified APIs, and all available hardware interfaces are documented.

Each subsystem is further divided into modules, where each module is dedicated to a specific task and provides an API to other software modules. The modules within the KronOS library are optional and can be included or excluded depending on system requirements. The system diagram clearly conveys which functionalities are enabled and available within the satellite's subsystems, without requiring a detailed examination of their internal implementations.

To keep the system manageable and maintain effective load balancing, no additional priority levels are introduced. While this model does not rely on formal schedulability analysis, it is conceptually aligned with the notion of robust priority assignment as defined in realtime systems literature [12].
A special layer, called the KronOS Task-Manager, extends the FreeRTOS scheduler with functionality for dynamic resource allocation, load balancing, and fault management.

Dynamic resources in the system include task-specific stack memory, available power from the EPS, and processor time. Each task receives its stack from a statically allocated heap managed by FreeRTOS. Power availability and power consumption are monitored to ensure stable operation.

Before a new task can be created, the system must be in a stable state. The required stack size is specified during task creation by the initiating process. This value is typically an estimate based on prior testing, with an added safety margin.

There are three possible outcomes: 1. Sufficient resources are available - the task is scheduled immediately. 2. Insufficient resources - the system attempts to free memory and processing capacity by terminating lower-priority tasks. 3. Insufficient resources with no lower-priority tasks available - if the new task is non-critical, it is rejected. If it is critical and still cannot be scheduled, the system enters a non-runnable state.

To incorporate power consumption into the loadbalancing process, the Task Manager receives regular external reports from the EPS. These reports include key parameters such as the current state of charge, overall power consumption, and charging current of the batteries. Within the Task Manager, trigger points are defined to respond to critical EPS values.

If a trigger point indicates a lack of power while only critical tasks are running, the system initiates a controlled shutdown to conserve energy. If non-critical tasks are still active, these are first moved to the suspended state before more drastic action is taken. Once sufficient power becomes available again, previously suspended tasks are resumed automatically. This mechanism, shown in Fig. 5, ensures that energy-critical situations are handled gracefully, maintaining essential system functionality while preventing instability.

In addition, each task is assigned an individual timeout that serves as an internal task watchdog. If a task stalls or becomes unresponsive, it is terminated by a dedicated health-check task (Fig. 6) and the allocated resources are released in a controlled manner.

Thus, a key benefit of MBSE lies in its ability to identify, at an early stage, which components of a system are vulnerable to concurrency issues such as thread preemption or interrupt handling. By employing formal verification within MBSE models, potential hazards can be detected more effectively during the design phase, significantly reducing debugging complexity in later implementation stages.

The Simulation-Driven Validation Tests are intended to validate the correct implementation of the system model and to reveal potential bugs and vulnerabilities in the design. A distinction is made between HIL and SIL tests. HIL tests aim to validate the integration of a system on actual hardware. Three types of test scenarios have been defined and conducted for the validation of failsafe mechanisms.

To evaluate the watchdog implementation, a KronOS instance with a dedicated watchdog task is executed on the OBC. The OBC incorporates two external watchdogs with a timeout of 1.6~seconds, enabling hot-swapping to a redundant processor or power source.

watchdog of the MSP430 is configured with a timeout of 1~second. During testing, a deliberate deadlock is introduced in a secondary task. This condition consistently causes the software watchdog to trigger after the 1-second timeout, initiating a soft reset of the processor. The experiment thereby validates that deadlocks are reliably detected and resolved through the watchdog mechanism, ensuring bounded-time recovery and system availability.
Tasks are created sequentially to deliberately trigger a stack overflow, a floating-point exception, and a null pointer exception.

In all tested cases, the faulty tasks are cleaned up by the task timeout mechanism (see Fig. 6), and the resources are released. Depending on the affected priority, the appropriate recovery strategy is executed.

An additional task simulates the reception of incorrectly encoded messages to evaluate the fault tolerance of the decoder. The experiment demonstrates that partially received or malformed messages are reliably discarded after a defined timeout. This timeout is configured according to the maximum transmission rate of the hardware channel and the maximum message length. By enforcing these bounds, the receiver buffer is freed in time to prevent denial-of-service conditions caused by buffer overflows.

The results demonstrate that combining Model-Based Systems Engineering with simulation-driven validation provides a systematic way to design and test fault-tolerant real-time software for CubeSats. Formal modelling exposes concurrency risks such as race conditions early in the development process, while SIL and HIL experiments confirm that watchdogs, fault injection handling, and message validation mechanisms can reliably recover from deadlocks, runtime faults, and corrupted inputs.

MBSE contributes by clarifying complex task interactions and making these critical mechanisms traceable and verifiable at the design stage. This structured approach shows that reliability in nanosatellite software can be achieved without sacrificing modularity or maintainability, even under highly constrained conditions.

At the same time, the effectiveness of MBSE is bounded by the quality of the models. Poorly specified or incomplete models will not yield better implementations than conventional ad hoc approaches. Moreover, issues can only be identified if they are explicitly represented in the models, and if complexity is abstracted to a level that remains comprehensible for all stakeholders. Thus, while MBSE improves transparency and reduces integration risks, it does not replace engineering judgment.

Future work will focus on characterizing and mitigating new concurrency issues that arise from multithreading and unpredictable runtime behaviour. The framework will be applied to systems of higher complexity with additional subsystems to evaluate scalability. Finally, accumulated experience will be distilled into best practices and documentation of common pitfalls, providing practical guidance for future CubeSat and small satellite developments.
